definition: Revise means to reconsider and make changes to something, especially a written work, in order to improve it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word revise. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know revise should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: After reading the judges' comments, Tomás stayed up late to revise his competition essay, cutting the weak opening and adding stronger evidence.
To tweak a draft is to make one or two tiny adjustments — far lighter than to revise it, which means rethinking the whole piece to improve it.
To overhaul a draft goes further than to revise it: you tear it down and rebuild it from the ground up.

Rework means to shape the material again from a fresh angle — a scene rebuilt around a different character, an essay reorganized around a new thesis. Revise is wider and calmer: reconsider the work and change whatever needs improving, large or small. All reworking is revising; much revising is gentler than reworking.

Amend means to alter something formally, usually to correct or improve it — laws, contracts, and official records are amended. Revise belongs to drafts and working texts: a writer reconsiders and changes their own pages to make them better. Parliaments amend a bill; writers revise a chapter.

Polish means to refine the small details until the writing shines — smoothing sentences, sharpening word choices, perfecting what already works. Revise can cut far deeper: reconsidering structure, arguments, and whole passages. Polishing is the finishing touch at the end; revising can rebuild the middle of the work.

The playwright spent the whole summer working to revise her second act: she reconsidered every scene, cut a character who slowed the story, and rewrote the ending twice before the script finally felt right.
She didn't just reread the act — she reconsidered it and made changes to improve it.
That combination of looking again and changing for the better is the heart of revise.

Revise is the standard word for improving a draft, and its related noun form is revision — both the act of revising and the changed draft itself.
One caution: in British English, revise can also mean to study for an exam; the SAT tests the 'rework a text to improve it' sense.

Two weeks before the launch, the review committee returned Amara's keynote draft covered in marginalia.
Some notes were small — a date wrong, a clumsy phrase.
Others were structural: the middle section buried the announcement the whole speech existed to make.
She began to revise that evening, not by decorating sentences but by reconsidering the draft top to bottom.
She cut the history lesson from the middle, moved the announcement to the second minute, and rewrote the ending to point at it.
The committee read the new draft in silence, and the chair wrote one word across the cover page: ready.
